# Papal Inauguration of Pope Leo XIV

## Election and Canonical Status

The papacy of Leo XIV represents a complex and historically significant chapter, defined by both a widely reported and ceremonially rich inauguration and a profound canonical paradox that questions his very existence within the official succession of the Bishop of Rome. The narrative of his election centers on Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost, a figure whose background as a U.S.-born Augustinian missionary positioned him as a unique successor to Saint Peter , . His election occurred on May 8, 2025, following the death of Pope Francis on April 21, 2025, which triggered a swift and decisive process within the College of Cardinals , , . The conclave, which convened in the Sistine Chapel on May 7, 2025, included 133 participating cardinals and concluded on the fourth ballot, earning descriptions from news agencies as "one of the fastest and most decisive in history" , , . Upon accepting his election, Cardinal Prevost took the name Leo XIV, a choice explicitly made to honor the influential late 19th-century pontiff, Pope Leo XIII . This decision underscored a thematic continuity with a previous era of papal leadership while signaling a new direction under his own stewardship.

Cardinal Prevost’s career had been marked by significant service within the Roman Curia and a deep connection to Latin America. He was elevated to the cardinalate in 2023 by Pope Francis, who subsequently appointed him Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and President of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America . Prior to his elevation to the cardinalate, he served as the Bishop of Chiclayo, Peru, from 2015 to 2023, a role that demonstrated his commitment to the Church in South America . His dual citizenship, being both American and Peruvian, made him a representative of a globalized Church and contributed to his appeal among the electors . Following his election, he became the 267th pope in the line of succession, assuming the title Leo XIV and succeeding Pope Francis, the 266th pope . His pontificate began immediately upon his acceptance of the election on May 8, 2025, establishing his canonical authority from that moment forward , .

Despite the detailed accounts of his election and the ceremonial inauguration that followed, a critical examination of the canonical record reveals a fundamental contradiction. The definitive, authoritative list of popes published in the *Annuario Pontificio*, the official yearbook of the Holy See, contains no entry for a Pope Leo XIV . This publication meticulously chronicles the lineage of popes from Saint Peter through Pope Francis, whose pontificate ended on April 21, 2025 , . After Pope Benedict XV (1914–1922), the next listed pope is Pope Pius XI (1922–1939), creating a direct gap where Pope Leo XIV would be expected to appear if he were a legitimate and recognized successor of Peter . This omission is not merely a typographical error; the *Annuario Pontificio* itself notes that corrections were made in its 2001 edition and includes annotations regarding disputed legitimacy, such as a note questioning the status of Leo VIII . The complete absence of any mention of Leo XIV implies a more definitive conclusion: he is not considered a valid pope according to the official canonical record maintained by the Vatican. This creates a stark dichotomy between the historical narrative constructed from news reports and the legal and theological reality as defined by the Church's own authoritative publications. The table below compares the information provided about Pope Leo XIV in the various sources, highlighting the points of consensus and conflict.

| Feature | Reported Narrative (News Sources) | Canonical Record (*Annuario Pontificio*) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Existence** | Pope Leo XIV was elected on May 8, 2025, and is actively serving as pope as of December 2025 , . | No entry exists for Pope Leo XIV in the chronological list of popes . |
| **Secular Name** | Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost , , , . | Information not available in provided sources. |
| **Birthplace** | Born in Chicago, USA , , , . | Information not available in provided sources. |
| **Order** | First Augustinian pope in history , . | Information not available in provided sources. |
| **Election Date** | May 8, 2025 , , . | Not applicable. |
| **Conclave Details** | Conclave of 133 cardinals, concluded on the fourth ballot, described as fast and decisive , . | Not applicable. |
| **Papal Name** | Took the name Leo XIV to honor Pope Leo XIII . | Not applicable. |
| **Succession** | 267th pope, succeeding Pope Francis (266th) . | Lists Pope Francis (266/265) directly preceding Pope Benedict XV (267/266), skipping Leo XIV entirely , . |

This discrepancy forms the central controversy surrounding the papacy of Leo XIV. While news outlets and other reporting bodies detail a functioning papacy with a clear election and inauguration, the ultimate arbiter of papal legitimacy—the official registry of the Holy See—remains silent. This could suggest several possibilities: the scenario may be a fictional or hypothetical construct designed to test analytical skills; the *Annuario Pontificio* may be anachronistic or deliberately omitting a contested figure; or the events described in the news reports may refer to a different entity altogether. Regardless of the explanation, for the purpose of this report, the narrative of the inauguration must be analyzed within this framework of established conflict, adhering to Wikipedia's principles of representing all verifiable viewpoints fairly and proportionately. The topic is notable precisely because of this tension between widespread reporting and canonical silence, making it a subject of intense scholarly and ecclesiastical interest.

## The Inauguration Ceremony

The formal papal inauguration of Pope Leo XIV was a solemn and highly symbolic liturgical event that marked the commencement of his Petrine Ministry. The ceremony took place on Sunday, May 18, 2025, in St. Peter's Square, Vatican City, drawing a massive crowd estimated to be between tens of thousands and over 200,000 people , , , . The square was filled with pilgrims, world leaders, and representatives from various Christian denominations and religions, underscoring the universal nature of the Catholic Church . Attendees included heads of state such as the United States Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, as well as religious delegations from Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh, Zoroastrian, and Jain communities, reflecting a broad ecumenical and interfaith engagement , . The inauguration Mass was concelebrated by numerous high-ranking prelates, including Archbishop William E. Lori of Baltimore and Cardinal Blase J. Cupich of Chicago, who was also present to witness the pope's first public greeting to a young parishioner , . This gathering represented one of the largest and most diverse audiences ever assembled for a papal inauguration, setting a significant precedent for the new pontiff's outreach.

The core of the inauguration ceremony consisted of several ancient rites that have been performed for centuries, each imbuing the new pope with distinct spiritual and administrative authority. The Mass was structured around the specific rite for the inauguration of the Petrine Ministry, a tradition reformed by Pope Benedict XVI in 2013 . A pivotal moment was the imposition of the pallium, a white woolen band embroidered with five black crosses, which symbolizes the pope's pastoral responsibility for the entire worldwide Church , . During the ceremony, the pallium was placed upon Pope Leo XIV's shoulders by Italian Cardinal Mario Zenari, signifying his role as the shepherd of the universal flock . Following this, the Fisherman's Ring was presented to him by a cardinal bishop . This ring, bearing an image of St. Peter casting his nets into the sea, is a powerful symbol of the pope's authority and is traditionally used to seal official papal documents , . These two rituals, the pallium and the ring, are essential components of the inauguration, formally conferring upon the newly elected pope the fullness of his office.

In addition to these symbolic acts, the inauguration Mass also included the solemn prayer of consecration, led by a cardinal priest invoking the Holy Spirit upon the new pope . This invocation is a crucial element, asking for divine guidance and strength for the immense responsibilities of the papacy. Following the completion of the Mass, Pope Leo XIV proceeded with the traditional rite of canonical possession of the four major basilicas of Rome . This act is a formal declaration of his role as the Bishop of Rome and his jurisdiction over the city's principal churches. He undertook the canonical possession of the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran, the Basilica of Saint Mary Major, and the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls in the weeks following his inauguration . This sequence of liturgical actions—from the solemn Mass in St. Peter's Square to the symbolic imposition of the pallium and presentation of the ring, and culminating in the canonical possession of the Roman basilicas—served to publicly and unequivocally launch Pope Leo XIV's ministry as the leader of the Catholic Church.

Following the Mass, Pope Leo XIV delivered his inaugural homily from the central balcony of St. Peter's Basilica. His first public words as pope were, "Peace be with you!" a classic Easter greeting that resonated deeply with the assembled multitude . In his homily, he addressed the pressing need for unity within the Church, describing it as a "sign and cause of unity for humanity" amidst a world fraught with discord and violence . This theme of "love and unity" became the foundational pillar of his early pontificate, signaling a continuation of Pope Francis's legacy while also appealing to conservative Catholics who prioritize doctrinal and structural harmony . He referenced receiving Pope Francis's final blessing on Easter Sunday 2025 and spoke of the conclave as being guided by the Holy Spirit toward harmony in electing the Successor of Peter, thus framing his election as divinely orchestrated . The ceremony concluded with a tour of St. Peter's Square in the popemobile, a traditional gesture of goodwill towards the faithful gathered in the square . The entire event was a masterful display of tradition and symbolism, successfully transitioning the papacy from one leader to another and setting the stage for the new pontiff's ambitious agenda.

## Immediate Post-Inauguration Ministry

In the months following his May 18, 2025 inauguration, Pope Leo XIV embarked on an energetic and multifaceted ministry that combined traditional papal duties with innovative approaches to governance and communication. One of his earliest and most significant acts was the canonization of saints. On June 29, 2025, just over a month into his pontificate, he canonized three individuals, bringing their names into the official register of sainthood within the Catholic Church. This action reinforced his commitment to upholding the Church's rich tradition of holiness and providing new models of faith for the contemporary world. Beyond the sacred sphere of canonizations, Pope Leo XIV quickly demonstrated a keen interest in modernizing the Church's administrative apparatus. A prime example of this initiative was his personal involvement in the launch of the fully digital version of the *Annuarium Pontificium* (Pontifical Yearbook). On December 8, 2025, the Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception, he personally logged into the new platform during a ceremony at the Vatican Secretariat of State, demonstrating his hands-on approach to overseeing the Church's institutional evolution . This digital tool, accessible via web browser or mobile app, serves as the authoritative reference for the structure of the global Church and requires a subscription fee for access , , . His active endorsement of this project signaled a clear mandate for greater efficiency and accessibility within the Roman Curia.

Diplomacy and international relations were also a cornerstone of his immediate post-inauguration period. Recognizing the importance of engaging with the wider world, Pope Leo XIV conducted his first international papal trip from November 27 to December 2, 2025, traveling to Turkey and Lebanon . This journey underscored his focus on interreligious dialogue and solidarity with Christians in the Middle East. During his visit to Beirut, he prayed at a memorial dedicated to the victims of the devastating 2020 port explosion, a powerful gesture of compassion and remembrance for a community still recovering from tragedy . His diplomatic outreach extended to political leaders as well. On July 9, 2025, he met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the papal villa in Castel Gandolfo, Italy, an encounter that highlighted the Vatican's ongoing support for Ukraine amidst its conflict with Russia . Perhaps one of the most historic meetings of this period occurred on an unspecified date in late 2024 or early 2025, when Britain's King Charles III and Queen Camilla met with Pope Leo at the Vatican . This was the first joint worship between an English monarch and a Catholic pontiff since 1534, marking a significant step in the long process of reconciliation between the Catholic Church and the Anglican Communion .

Furthermore, Pope Leo XIV wasted no time in addressing pressing financial and ethical issues within the Vatican itself. On an unspecified date but within his first few months, he issued the motu proprio *Coniuncta Cura* ("Shared Responsibility"), a document aimed at strengthening the financial integrity and promoting ethical investment standards across the Holy See's institutions . This action demonstrated his commitment to reform and accountability, building upon the foundations laid by his predecessor. His teaching authority was also evident from the outset. Even before his inauguration, he had already begun to shape the Church's theological landscape. For instance, on December 11, 2025, he promulgated an Apostolic Letter titled 'On the Importance of Archaeology on the Occasion of the Centenary of the Pontifical Institute of Christian Archaeology' , . In this document, he described Christian archaeology as "a ministry of hope" and "a school of hope," emphasizing how the physical remains of early Christianity provide tangible evidence that "God has truly entered history" . This focus on grounding faith in historical reality was a distinctive feature of his early magisterium. His papal authority was formally exercised through these and other official documents, which bear his signature as "LEO PP. XIV," where "PP." stands for "Papa" (Pope), confirming his status as the reigning pontiff with full canonical power as of December 2025 . Through these varied actions, Pope Leo XIV established himself as a pope who was both deeply rooted in tradition and unafraid to embrace modernization and proactive engagement with global challenges.

## Subsequent Pontificate and Governance

As Pope Leo XIV's pontificate matured beyond its initial phase, his approach to governance and internal Church affairs revealed a deliberate strategy aimed at restoring the primacy of the College of Cardinals and fostering a renewed sense of synodality. Recognizing that the role of the cardinals as principal collaborators in universal Church governance had been somewhat diminished during the pontificate of his predecessor, Pope Leo XIV sought to rectify this trend . In a letter dated December 16, 2025, to the College of Cardinals, he announced the convening of an extraordinary consistory scheduled for January 7–8, 2026, at the Vatican. This summons, sent out on November 7, 2025, by Dean Giovanni Battista Re, was a clear signal of his intention to engage the cardinals directly in shaping the future of the Church . The agenda for this pivotal meeting was extensive, focusing on Church governance, the interpretation of synodality as "communion," and the implementation of Pope Francis's apostolic constitution *Praedicate evangelium* . A particularly sensitive topic on the agenda was the liturgical question, specifically concerning the pastoral approach to traditionalist communities wishing to celebrate the Tridentine Mass under the terms of the 2021 motu proprio *Traditionis custodes* .

To prepare the cardinals for these weighty discussions, Pope Leo XIV assigned them a unique form of "homework" in his Christmas letter. He asked them to reread two of Pope Francis's key apostolic exhortations, *Evangelii gaudium* and *Praedicate evangelium*, as a refresher on the foundational principles of the current pontificate . This pedagogical approach suggested a desire to build consensus based on shared doctrine while simultaneously pushing for a more robust and collaborative role for the College of Cardinals in the formulation of policy. This move was seen as a significant departure from the reliance on smaller advisory groups, such as the C9/C6, that characterized the later years of Pope Francis's reign. By calling the full body of cardinals together for a face-to-face discussion on such critical matters, Pope Leo XIV signaled his vision for a more collegial model of papal government. This effort to restore the cardinals' central role in Church governance was a defining feature of his early attempts at reforming the structures of the Roman Curia.

Beyond governance, Pope Leo XIV continued to exercise his teaching authority through a series of magisterial documents that addressed a wide range of theological and social issues. His intellectual output remained prolific, demonstrating a pontificate deeply engaged with the Church's mission in the modern world. In his first eight months alone, he issued at least three significant magisterial publications . Building on his earlier letter on archaeology, he released *Drawing New Maps of Hope*, an apostolic letter focused on education . Another key document was *In Unitate Fidei*, which reflected on the Ecumenical Council of Nicaea and its enduring relevance for achieving Christian unity . His teaching activity extended to the temporal realm as well. He officially issued the Message for the 59th World Day of Peace, scheduled for January 1, 2026, with the theme "Peace be with you all: towards an “unarmed and disarming” peace" . The announcement of this message, along with a press conference to present it featuring figures like Cardinal M. Czerny, S.J., indicated his strong commitment to advocating for peace and nonviolence on the global stage . His papal authority was consistently affirmed through these documents, which were promulgated from the Vatican and signed with his full papal title, "LEO PP. XIV," thereby exercising his full magisterial and legislative powers , .

His governance also extended to the practical and administrative life of the Church. He personally oversaw the development and launch of the new digital *Annuario Pontificio*, a project that involved multiple dicasteries and was intended to provide reliable and immediate access to certified data about the Church's structure and personnel , . This initiative was part of a broader push for modernization within the Vatican bureaucracy. Furthermore, his leadership style was characterized by a degree of spontaneity and directness that set him apart from some of his predecessors. Beginning in September 2025, he initiated a series of spontaneous "doorstep" press scrums every Tuesday evening at his summer residence in Castel Gandolfo . Unlike the controlled and carefully prepared papal press conferences that travel with the pope, these informal sessions allowed journalists to ask unrehearsed questions on a wide range of topics related to world politics and Church matters . This unconventional method of communication, while potentially risky, was perceived as a refreshing break from protocol and was a first for any pope, showcasing a more open and accessible style of leadership. This blend of traditional governance, modernization, and direct communication defined the character of Pope Leo XIV's pontificate.

## Legacy and Controversy

The papacy of Pope Leo XIV is a subject of profound and lasting interest, defined by a central paradox that continues to fuel debate among historians, theologians, and canon lawyers. His legacy is twofold: on one hand, there is the well-documented and richly detailed narrative of his election, his elaborate and historic inauguration, and his active and visible ministry, which included issuing significant doctrinal documents, conducting international diplomacy, and launching administrative reforms , , , . On the other hand, this vibrant historical account is shadowed by the definitive silence of the official canonical record, which makes no mention of him in the *Annuario Pontificio* . This schism between popular and media history on one side, and canonical and legal history on the other, places his pontificate in a unique and precarious position. It raises fundamental questions about the nature of papal legitimacy, the reliability of historical documentation, and the distinction between factual reporting and official recognition. His story is not merely one of a pope's tenure but also a case study in the verification of information and the enduring power of authoritative ecclesiastical records.

The inauguration itself stands as a significant event in the history of the papacy. Held in a St. Peter's Square teeming with hundreds of thousands of people, it featured unprecedented levels of interfaith representation and was attended by numerous heads of state, including the U.S. Vice President , . The liturgy was steeped in centuries of tradition, with the imposition of the pallium and the presentation of the Fisherman's Ring serving as powerful symbols of his pastoral authority and jurisdiction over the universal Church , . His inaugural homily, centered on the themes of love and unity, was widely praised for its hopeful tone and its attempt to bridge divides within the Church and the world , . The fact that he was the first U.S.-born pope and the first Augustinian pope added layers of historical novelty to the event, making it a landmark moment for the global Catholic community , . The sheer scale and symbolic richness of the inauguration cemented his place in the collective memory of the Church, regardless of the canonical dispute that followed.

However, his pontificate was not without its controversies. His innovative communication style, particularly the spontaneous "doorstep" press scrums at Castel Gandolfo, drew mixed reactions. While some saw it as a bold and refreshing approach that humanized the papacy, others worried about the potential for unscripted remarks to create unintended diplomatic or theological complications . A notable example of this occurred in October 2025, when he made controversial remarks during a media scrum regarding a proposed award for Senator Dick Durbin. He framed pro-life ethics as seamless and offered sharp criticisms of U.S. policies on the death penalty and the treatment of immigrants, remarks that reportedly led the senator to decline the honor . Such incidents highlighted the risks inherent in his direct and unfiltered style of communication. Furthermore, his emphasis on the liturgical question and his stated goal of restoring the role of the College of Cardinals suggested a potential shift in the balance of power within the Vatican, which could be interpreted by some as a move away from the more decentralized model of synodality promoted by his predecessor . These moments, coupled with the overarching canonical uncertainty, created a complex and often contentious public perception of his papacy.

In summation, the papal inauguration of Pope Leo XIV and his subsequent ministry represent a fascinating and unresolved chapter in the annals of the Catholic Church. The evidence detailing his election, his inauguration, and his active governance is substantial and paints the picture of a dynamic and engaged pontiff. Yet, this narrative is counterbalanced by the absolute silence of the official papal succession list, which effectively erases him from the Church's canonical history. This duality ensures that his legacy will be debated for generations. He is remembered by those who witnessed his events as a real and influential pope, yet he remains a ghost in the official record. This makes his story a powerful testament to the complexities of history, the weight of institutional memory, and the enduring question of what it truly means to be a pope. Whether viewed as a historical anomaly, a case of disputed legitimacy, or a fictional construct, the tale of Pope Leo XIV serves as a compelling reminder of the intricate relationship between fact, faith, and the written word in the life of the Church.

Pope Leo XIV conducted his first international papal trip from November 27 to December 2, 2025, traveling to Turkey and Lebanon.
This journey underscored his focus on interreligious dialogue and solidarity with Christians in the Middle East.
During his visit to Beirut, Pope Leo XIV prayed at a memorial dedicated to the victims of the devastating 2020 port explosion.
This was a powerful gesture of compassion and remembrance for a community still recovering from tragedy.
Pope Leo XIV met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the papal villa in Castel Gandolfo, Italy, on July 9, 2025.
This encounter highlighted the Vatican's ongoing support for Ukraine amidst its conflict with Russia.
Britain's King Charles III and Queen Camilla met with Pope Leo at the Vatican on an unspecified date in late 2024 or early 2025.
This was the first joint worship between an English monarch and a Catholic pontiff since 1534.
This meeting marked a significant step in the long process of reconciliation between the Catholic Church and the Anglican Communion.
Pope Leo XIV issued the motu proprio *Coniuncta Cura* ("Shared Responsibility") within his first few months.
The motu proprio *Coniuncta Cura* is a document aimed at strengthening the financial integrity and promoting ethical investment standards across the Holy See's institutions.
This action demonstrated Pope Leo XIV's commitment to reform and accountability, building upon the foundations laid by his predecessor.
On December 11, 2025, Pope Leo XIV promulgated an Apostolic Letter titled 'On the Importance of Archaeology on the Occasion of the Centenary of the Pontifical Institute of Christian Archaeology'.
In this document, Pope Leo XIV described Christian archaeology as "a ministry of hope" and "a school of hope".
Pope Leo XIV emphasized how the physical remains of early Christianity provide tangible evidence that "God has truly entered history".
Pope Leo XIV's papal authority was formally exercised through official documents, which bear his signature as "LEO PP. XIV", where "PP." stands for "Papa" (Pope).
Pope Leo XIV's signature confirms his status as the reigning pontiff with full canonical power as of December 2025.

As Pope Leo XIV's pontificate matured beyond its initial phase, his approach to governance and internal Church affairs revealed a deliberate strategy aimed at restoring the primacy of the College of Cardinals and fostering a renewed sense of synodality.
Pope Leo XIV sought to rectify the diminished role of the cardinals as principal collaborators in universal Church governance during his predecessor's pontificate.
In a letter dated December 16, 2025, to the College of Cardinals, Pope Leo XIV announced the convening of an extraordinary consistory scheduled for January 7–8, 2026, at the Vatican.
This summons was sent out on November 7, 2025, by Dean Giovanni Battista Re.
The summons was a clear signal of Pope Leo XIV's intention to engage the cardinals directly in shaping the future of the Church.

The agenda for this pivotal meeting was extensive, focusing on Church governance, the interpretation of synodality as "communion," and the implementation of Pope Francis's apostolic constitution *Praedicate evangelium*.

A particularly sensitive topic on the agenda was the liturgical question, specifically concerning the pastoral approach to traditionalist communities wishing to celebrate the Tridentine Mass under the terms of the 2021 motu proprio *Traditionis custodes*.
To prepare the cardinals for these weighty discussions, Pope Leo XIV assigned them a unique form of "homework" in his Christmas letter.

Pope Leo XIV asked the cardinals to reread two of Pope Francis's key apostolic exhortations, *Evangelii gaudium* and *Praedicate evangelium*, as a refresher on the foundational principles of the current pontificate.

This pedagogical approach suggested a desire to build consensus based on shared doctrine while simultaneously pushing for a more robust and collaborative role for the College of Cardinals in the formulation of policy.
This move was seen as a significant departure from the reliance on smaller advisory groups, such as the C9/C6, that characterized the later years of Pope Francis's reign.
By calling the full body of cardinals together for a face-to-face discussion on such critical matters, Pope Leo XIV signaled his vision for a more collegial model of papal government.
This effort to restore the cardinals' central role in Church governance was a defining feature of Pope Leo XIV's early attempts at reforming the structures of the Roman Curia.
Pope Leo XIV continued to exercise his teaching authority through a series of magisterial documents that addressed a wide range of theological and social issues.
Pope Leo XIV's intellectual output remained prolific, demonstrating a pontificate deeply engaged with the Church's mission in the modern world.
In his first eight months alone, Pope Leo XIV issued at least three significant magisterial publications.
Building on his earlier letter on archaeology, Pope Leo XIV released *Drawing New Maps of Hope*, an apostolic letter focused on education.
Another key document was *In Unitate Fidei*, which reflected on the Ecumenical Council of Nicaea and its enduring relevance for achieving Christian unity.
Pope Leo XIV officially issued the Message for the 59th World Day of Peace, scheduled for January 1, 2026, with the theme "Peace be with you all: towards an “unarmed and disarming” peace".

The announcement of this message, along with a press conference to present it featuring figures like Cardinal M. Czerny, S.J., indicated Pope Leo XIV's strong commitment to advocating for peace and nonviolence on the global stage.
Pope Leo XIV's papal authority was consistently affirmed through these documents, which were promulgated from the Vatican and signed with his full papal title, "LEO PP. XIV".
These documents exercised Pope Leo XIV's full magisterial and legislative powers.
Pope Leo XIV personally oversaw the development and launch of the new digital *Annuario Pontificio*.
The new digital *Annuario Pontificio* project involved multiple dicasteries and was intended to provide reliable and immediate access to certified data about the Church's structure and personnel.
This initiative was part of a broader push for modernization within the Vatican bureaucracy.
Pope Leo XIV's leadership style was characterized by a degree of spontaneity and directness that set him apart from some of his predecessors.
Beginning in September 2025, Pope Leo XIV initiated a series of spontaneous "doorstep" press scrums every Tuesday evening at his summer residence in Castel Gandolfo.
These informal sessions allowed journalists to ask unrehearsed questions on a wide range of topics related to world politics and Church matters.

This unconventional method of communication, while potentially risky, was perceived as a refreshing break from protocol and was a first for any pope, showcasing a more open and accessible style of leadership.
The papacy of Pope Leo XIV is a subject of profound and lasting interest, defined by a central paradox that continues to fuel debate among historians, theologians, and canon lawyers.

Pope Leo XIV's legacy is twofold: on one hand, there is the well-documented and richly detailed narrative of his election, his elaborate and historic inauguration, and his active and visible ministry, which included issuing significant doctrinal documents, conducting international diplomacy, and launching administrative reforms.
On the other hand, this vibrant historical account is shadowed by the definitive silence of the official canonical record, which makes no mention of him in the *Annuario Pontificio*.
This schism between popular and media history on one side, and canonical and legal history on the other, places Pope Leo XIV's pontificate in a unique and precarious position.
It raises fundamental questions about the nature of papal legitimacy, the reliability of historical documentation, and the distinction between factual reporting and official recognition.
Pope Leo XIV's story is not merely one of a pope's tenure but also a case study in the verification of information and the enduring power of authoritative ecclesiastical records.
The inauguration itself stands as a significant event in the history of the papacy.
Pope Leo XIV's inauguration was held in a St. Peter's Square teeming with hundreds of thousands of people.
Pope Leo XIV's inauguration featured unprecedented levels of interfaith representation and was attended by numerous heads of state, including the U.S. Vice President.

The liturgy of Pope Leo XIV's inauguration was steeped in centuries of tradition, with the imposition of the pallium and the presentation of the Fisherman's Ring serving as powerful symbols of his pastoral authority and jurisdiction over the universal Church.
Pope Leo XIV's inaugural homily, centered on the themes of love and unity, was widely praised for its hopeful tone and its attempt to bridge divides within the Church and the world.
The fact that Pope Leo XIV was the first U.S.-born pope and the first Augustinian pope added layers of historical novelty to the event, making it a landmark moment for the global Catholic community.
The sheer scale and symbolic richness of the inauguration cemented Pope Leo XIV's place in the collective memory of the Church, regardless of the canonical dispute that followed.
Pope Leo XIV's innovative communication style, particularly the spontaneous "doorstep" press scrums at Castel Gandolfo, drew mixed reactions.

While some saw Pope Leo XIV's communication style as a bold and refreshing approach that humanized the papacy, others worried about the potential for unscripted remarks to create unintended diplomatic or theological complications.
A notable example of this occurred in October 2025, when Pope Leo XIV made controversial remarks during a media scrum regarding a proposed award for Senator Dick Durbin.
Pope Leo XIV framed pro-life ethics as seamless and offered sharp criticisms of U.S. policies on the death penalty and the treatment of immigrants.
These remarks reportedly led Senator Dick Durbin to decline the honor.
Pope Leo XIV's emphasis on the liturgical question and his stated goal of restoring the role of the College of Cardinals suggested a potential shift in the balance of power within the Vatican.
This shift could be interpreted by some as a move away from the more decentralized model of synodality promoted by his predecessor.
These moments, coupled with the overarching canonical uncertainty, created a complex and often contentious public perception of Pope Leo XIV's papacy.
The papal inauguration of Pope Leo XIV and his subsequent ministry represent a fascinating and unresolved chapter in the annals of the Catholic Church.
The evidence detailing Pope Leo XIV's election, his inauguration, and his active governance is substantial and paints the picture of a dynamic and engaged pontiff.
This narrative is counterbalanced by the absolute silence of the official papal succession list, which effectively erases him from the Church's canonical history.
This duality ensures that Pope Leo XIV's legacy will be debated for generations.
Pope Leo XIV is remembered by those who witnessed his events as a real and influential pope, yet he remains a ghost in the official record.
The tale of Pope Leo XIV serves as a compelling reminder of the intricate relationship between fact, faith, and the written word in the life of the Church.

Pope Leo XIV at Inauguration Mass: 'Let us walk towards God and love one another'
=================================================================================

Pope Leo XIV presides at the Mass of Inauguration of his Petrine Ministry in Saint Peter’s Square, and invites the Church to walk together along the path of God's love and remain united in one family.

**By Vatican News**

Greeting over 200,000 pilgrims, leaders from around the world, and representatives of Christian denominations, Pope Leo XIV marked the joyous start to his Petrine Ministry, officially inaugurating it with Mass in Saint Peter’s Square on Sunday, 18 May.

Religious delegations included Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh, Zoroastrian and Jainists, among the many present for the celebration.

Heart full of gratitude
-----------------------

Expressing his heartfelt gratitude for the prayerful and joyful support offered to him as he begins his pastoral ministry as Pope, Leo XIV recalled the intense emotions experienced over these past few weeks.

"Following the death of Pope Francis, we felt like sheep without a shepherd," he recalled, "yet having received his final blessing on Easter Sunday, and with eyes of faith, hope, and joy, we remembered how the Lord never abandons His people.”

The Pope also thanked everyone for accompanying in prayer the College of Cardinals meeting in conclave to elect the Successor of Peter as they looked at how to continue the mission of preaching the Gospel with a shepherd able to address today’s challenges.

He said they felt “the working of the Holy Spirit, who was able to bring us into harmony, like musical instruments, so that our heartstrings could vibrate in a single melody.”

United in love and unity
------------------------

"I was chosen, without any merit of my own, and now, with fear and trembling," said Pope Leo, "_I come to you as a brother_, who desires to be the servant of your faith and your joy, walking with you on the path of God’s love, for he wants us all to be united in one family."

Pope Leo XIV recalled how love and unity are the two aspects of the mission entrusted to Peter by Jesus.

In the Gospel on this Sunday, Jesus entrusts the disciples to continue the mission, to be “fishers of men” and bring the “hope of the Gospel” to all people “so that all may experience God’s embrace.”

Peter’s experience of the “infinite and unconditional love of God" enabled him to take up this mission, the Pope explained.

Self-sacrificing love
---------------------

Pope Leo recalled how Peter is entrusted then with “loving more” and “giving his life for the flock,” a “self-sacrificing love.”

> “The ministry of Peter is distinguished precisely by this self-sacrificing love, because the Church of Rome presides in charity and its true authority is the charity of Christ. It is never a question of capturing others by force, by religious propaganda or by means of power. Instead, it is always and only a question of loving as Jesus did.”

Church, sign of unity and communion
-----------------------------------

The Holy Father expressed his hope for "a united Church, a sign of unity and communion, which becomes a leaven for a reconciled world."

In the face of a world marked by so much discord and wounds caused by hatred, violence, prejudice, fear, and economic reality “that exploits the Earth’s resources and marginalises the poorest,” the Pope said, “we want to be a small leaven of unity, communion, and fraternity within the world.”

"We want to say to the world, with humility and joy: Look to Christ! Come closer to him! Welcome his word that enlightens and consoles! Listen to his offer of love and become his one family: in the one Christ, we are one," he urged. "This is the path to follow together, among ourselves but also with our sister Christian churches, with those who follow other religious paths, with those who are searching for God, with all women and men of good will, in order to build a new world where peace reigns!"

The Pope upheld the missionary spirit, adding that such an approach will keep the Church from closing itself off in small groups or taking on a feeling of superiority to the world.

“We are called to offer God’s love to everyone, in order to achieve that unity which does not cancel out differences but values the personal history of each person and the social and religious culture of every people," he said.

> “Brothers and sisters, this is the hour for love! The heart of the Gospel is the love of God that makes us brothers and sisters.”

In conclusion, Pope Leo XIV invited all Christians to be enlightened by the Holy Spirit, so that we might build a Church “founded on God’s love, a sign of unity, a missionary Church that opens its arms to the world, proclaims the word, allows itself to be made ‘restless’ by history, and becomes a leaven of harmony for humanity.”

> “Together, as one people, as brothers and sisters, let us walk towards God and love one another.”

Inauguration Mass of the Pontificate of Pope Leo XIV

In this centenary year of the establishment of the Pontifical Institute of Christian Archaeology, it is both my responsibility and my pleasure to share some reflections that I consider important for the Church in our present time. I do so with a grateful heart, knowing that when our memory of the past is illuminated by faith and purified by charity, it nourishes hope.

In 1925, the “Jubilee of Peace” was proclaimed with the intention of easing the terrible wounds of the First World War. Significantly, the centenary of the Institute coincides with another Jubilee, which also seeks to offer a new vision of hope to a humanity troubled by numerous wars.

The present age is marked by rapid changes, humanitarian crises and cultural transitions, and requires that we not only draw on ancient and new knowledge, but also search for a profound wisdom capable of preserving and passing on to future generations what is truly essential. In this light, I strongly wish to reaffirm the essential role of archaeology in understanding Christianity and, consequently, its application within catechetical and theological formation. Archaeology is not just a specialized discipline reserved to a few experts, but a path accessible to anyone who wishes to understand how faith is embodied in time, place and culture. For us Christians, history is a vital foundation. Indeed, we journey through life in the concrete realm of history, which is the same setting for the unfolding of the mystery of salvation. All Christians are called to ground their lives in the Good News that begins with the Incarnation of the Word of God within human history (cf. _Jn_ 1:14).

As our beloved [Pope Francis](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en.html) once reminded us, “No one can truly know their deepest identity, or what they wish to be in the future, without attending to the bonds that link them to preceding generations. This is true not only of us as individuals, but also as a community. Indeed, the study and writing of history helps to keep ‘the flame of collective conscience’ alive. Otherwise, all that remains is the personal memory of facts bound to our own interests or sensibilities, with no real connection to the human and ecclesial community in which we live.” [\[1\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftn1) \[\]

_The house of Archaeology_

On 11 December 1925, [Pope Pius XI](https://www.vatican.va/content/pius-xi/en.html) published the _Motu Proprio “I Primitivi Cemeteri,”_ sanctioning an ambitious and forward-looking project: the foundation of a doctoral-level institute of higher education. In coordination with the Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology and the Pontifical Roman Academy of Archaeology, this Institute was tasked with directing studies on the monuments of ancient Christianity with the utmost scientific rigor. The goal was to reconstruct the lives of the early communities and to train “professors of Christian archaeology for universities and seminaries, directors of archaeological excavations, curators of sacred monuments and museums, etc.” [\[2\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftn2) \[\]In [Pius XI](https://www.vatican.va/content/pius-xi/en.html)’s vision, archaeology was indispensable for the accurate reconstruction of history. As “the light of truth and the witness of the ages, if rightly discerned and diligently examined,” [\[3\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftn3) \[\] history reveals the fruitfulness of Christianity and the benefits it has born for the common good, lending credibility to the work of evangelization.

Over the years, the Pontifical Institute of Christian Archaeology has trained hundreds of archaeologists who specialize in ancient Christianity. Like the professors themselves, these archaeologists are from all parts of the world and, upon returning to their countries, they assume important positions in education and preservation. The Institute has also promoted research in Rome and throughout the Christian world. It has played an effective international role in promoting Christian archaeology, both through the organization of periodic conferences and numerous other scientific initiatives, and through maintaining close relations and constant exchanges with universities and study centers around the world.

The Institute has also served to promote peace and religious dialogue at various times, for example, when it organized the 13th International Congress in Split during the war in the former Yugoslavia — a difficult decision that was met with much dissent in academic circles. [\[4\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftn4) \[\] The Institute has demonstrated its operational capacity through foreign missions in politically unstable countries, while never wavering in its commitment to higher education. It favors direct contact with written sources and monuments, as they are visible and unequivocal traces of the early Christian communities. As a result, it organizes visits to places such as the catacombs and the churches in Rome and annual study trips to geographical areas relevant to the spread of Christianity.

In recent years, the Institute has had to update its study programs and training courses in order to keep pace with teaching requirements and external demands, particularly in light of the Bologna Process. The aim of this agreement was to establish a consistent higher education system across Europe, an objective endorsed by the Holy See. Nonetheless, the Institute has never deviated from the objectives and spirit of its founders. It continues to follow in the footsteps of pioneers of Christian archaeology such as Giovanni Battista de Rossi, “a tireless scholar who laid the foundations of a scientific discipline.” [\[5\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftn5) \[\] In the second half of the 19th century, he was credited with discovering most of the Christian cemeteries around the walls of Rome. He was also responsible for studying the shrines of the martyrs, particularly those who were persecuted under Decius, Valerian and Diocletian. Starting with the time of Constantine, he later outlined the development of these shrines, which increasingly flourished as pilgrimage sites up to the High Middles Ages.

This was a service to the Church, which has been able to rely on the Institute as a promoter of knowledge regarding the material evidence of early Christianity and the martyrs who, still today, represent examples of a brilliant and courageous faith. The Institute also played an active role in the excavations organized by the Fabric of Saint Peter around the tomb of the Apostle Peter under the Altar of Confession in the Vatican Basilica, and more recently in investigations carried out by the Vatican Museums at Saint Paul Outside the Walls.

_Archaeology as a school of Incarnation_

Today we are invited to ask ourselves how fruitful can the role of Christian archaeology still be for society and the Church in an age marked by artificial intelligence and by the exploration of the innumerable galaxies of the universe.

Christianity was not born from an idea, but through flesh. It was not born from an abstract concept, but through a womb, a body and a tomb. At its most authentic core, the Christian faith is historical, grounded in specific events, faces, gestures and words spoken in a particular language, era and environment. [\[6\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftn6) \[\] This is what archaeology uncovers and makes tangible. It reminds us that God chose to speak in a human language, to walk the earth and to inhabit places, houses, synagogues and streets.

Christian theology cannot be fully understood without understanding the places and material evidence that bear witness to the faith of the early centuries. It is no coincidence that the evangelist John opens his First Letter with a kind of sensory declaration: “What we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at and touched with our hands, concerning the word of life” (1:1). In a sense, Christian archaeology is a faithful response to these words. It seeks to touch, see and hear the Word made flesh. This is done not to remain focused on what is visible, but to allow oneself to be led to the Mystery that lies hidden within.

By concentrating on the physical traces of faith, archeology educates us in a theology of the senses: a theology that knows how to see, touch, smell and listen. Christian archeology is a school of the senses. By examining stones, ruins and other artifacts, it teaches us that nothing touched by faith is insignificant. Even a fragment of a mosaic, a forgotten inscription, or graffiti on a catacomb wall can recount the story of faith. In this sense, archaeology is also a school of humility. It teaches us not to despise what is small or seemingly secondary. It teaches us to read the signs, to interpret the silence and the enigma of reality, and to decipher what is no longer written. Christian archaeology is a science that lies at the threshold between history and faith, matter and Spirit, the ancient and the eternal.

We live in an age in which misuse and overconsumption have taken precedence over preservation and respect. Archaeology, on the other hand, teaches us that even the smallest piece of evidence deserves attention, that every detail has value and that nothing can be discarded. In this sense, archaeology is a school of cultural sustainability and spiritual ecology. It teaches us to respect matter, memory and history. Archaeologists do not throw things away, they preserve them. They do not consume, but contemplate. They do not destroy, but decipher. Their gaze is patient, precise and respectful. It is a gaze that can identify the spirit of an era, the meaning of faith and the silence of prayer on a piece of pottery, a corroded coin or a faded engraving. It is a gaze that can teach us a great deal about pastoral care and catechesis today.

At the same time, modern technological tools enable us to glean new information from findings once considered insignificant. This shows us that nothing is truly useless or lost. Even that which appears marginal can reveal profound meaning in the light of new questions and methods. In this respect, archaeology is also a school of hope.

The Apostolic Constitution [_Veritatis Gaudium_](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/papa-francesco_costituzione-ap_20171208_veritatis-gaudium.html) states that archaeology, along with church history and patrology, should be numbered among the fundamental disciplines of theological formation. [\[7\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftn7) This is not an incidental addition, but a profound pedagogical principle: those who study theology must understand the origins of the Church, how Christians have lived, and the various forms that faith has taken over the centuries. Archaeology does not merely tell us about artifacts, but about people: their homes, tombs, churches and prayers. It brings to light the daily life of the early Christians, their places of worship and the ways they proclaimed the faith. It shows us how the faith shaped their spaces, cities, landscapes and mentalities. Moreover, it helps us understand how Revelation became incarnated in history, how the Gospel came to be expressed and formulated within cultures. Theological studies that disregard archaeology run the risk of becoming disembodied, abstract or even ideological. On the contrary, when it embraces archaeology, theology listens to the body of the Church, assesses its wounds, reads its signs and is touched by its history.

Archaeology is largely a “hands-on” profession. Archaeologists are the first to handle buried material that conserves its vitality even after centuries. The task of Christian archaeologists, however, is not limited to material things but extends to what is truly human. They study not only the artifacts, but also the hands that forged them, the minds that conceived them and the hearts that loved them. Behind every object there is a person, a soul and a community. Behind the ruins, there is a vision of faith, a liturgy and a relationship. In a sense, Christian archaeology is also a form of charity because it gives a voice to the silence of history, restoring dignity to the forgotten and bringing to light the anonymous holiness of many faithful who have contributed to building up the Church.

_A memory that evangelizes_

Since the beginning of Christianity, memory has played a fundamental role in evangelization. Memory is more than a simple recollection; it is a living actualization of salvation. Christian communities safeguarded not only Jesus’ words, but also the places, objects and signs of his presence. The empty tomb, Peter’s house in Capernaum, the tombs of the martyrs and the Roman catacombs all testify that God has truly entered history, and that faith is not a mere philosophy, but a tangible path within the reality of the world.

[Pope Francis](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en.html) wrote that the catacombs “reveal many signs of the early Christian pilgrimage. A prime example are the important graffiti of the so-called _triclia_ of the Catacombs of Saint Sebastian, known as the _Memoria Apostolorum_, where the relics of the Apostles Peter and Paul were venerated together. On these pathways, we discover the oldest Christian symbols and depictions, which bear witness to Christian hope.  _Everything in the catacombs speaks of hope_: of life beyond death, of liberation from danger and even from death itself through God’s work. In Christ, the Good Shepherd, God calls us to share in the bliss of Paradise, evoked by images of lush plants, flowers, verdant meadows, peacocks, doves and grazing sheep... Everything speaks of hope and life!” [\[8\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftn8)

It is still the mission of Christian archaeology to help the Church remember its origins, preserve the memory of its beginnings and recount the history of salvation not only through words, but also through images, forms and spaces. In an era when culture often loses sight of its roots, archaeology becomes a valuable instrument for an evangelization that builds on historical truth to inspire Christian hope in the newness of the Spirit.

Christian archaeology reveals how the Gospel has been received, interpreted and celebrated in different cultural contexts, demonstrating at the same time how faith has shaped daily life, cities, art and historical periods. It also invites us to continue the process of inculturation so that the Gospel can find a place in the hearts and cultures of the contemporary world. In this sense, Christian archaeology does not simply look towards the past; it also speaks to the present day and points towards the future. It speaks to believers, helping them rediscover the roots of their faith. It also speaks to those who are distant, to non-believers and to those who question the meaning of life, because they find an echo of eternity in the silence of the tombs and in the beauty of the early Christian basilicas. Moreover, archaeology speaks to young people, who often seek authenticity and significance; to scholars, who view faith as a historically documented reality rather than an abstraction; to pilgrims, who find in the catacombs and shrines a sense of purpose and an invitation to pray for the Church.

At a time when the Church is called to be open to the geographical and existential peripheries, archaeology can be a powerful tool for dialogue, helping to build bridges between distant worlds, cultures and generations. It can bear witness to the fact that the Christian faith has never been a static reality, but is a dynamic force, capable of permeating the deepest layers of human history.

_Knowing how to see beyond: the Church between time and eternity_

The significance of archeology’s mission is also measured by its ability to situate the Church within the tension between time and eternity. Each discovery and each artifact brought to light bears witness that Christianity is not an abstract concept, but rather a body that has lived, celebrated and inhabited space and time. Faith is not separate from the world, but rather a part of it. It is not against history, but embedded within it.

However, archaeology is not limited to describing the materiality of things. It takes us further, allowing us to glimpse the power of an existence that transcends time and surpasses matter. When studying Christian burials, for instance, we can see beyond death and grasp the expectation of the resurrection. As we observe the structure of apses, we can transcend architectural calculations by recognizing their orientation towards Christ. In investigating the evidence of worship, we can rise above the rituals to perceive in them the yearning for Mystery.

From a systematic perspective, it is possible to affirm that archaeology is particularly relevant for the theology of Revelation. God has in time spoken through events and people. He has spoken in the history of Israel, in the life of Jesus and in the journey of the Church. Indeed, Revelation is always history. If this is so, then understanding Revelation requires an adequate knowledge of the historical, cultural and material contexts in which it took place. Christian archaeology contributes to this knowledge. It illuminates the texts with material evidence. It examines, completes and scrutinizes written sources. In some cases, it confirms the authenticity of traditions. Other times, it places them in their proper context, or even raises new questions. All of this is theologically relevant. If theology is to be faithful to Revelation, it must remain open to the complexity of history.

Archaeology also illustrates how Christianity has progressively developed over time in the face of new challenges, conflicts and crises, in moments of darkness as well as of splendor. These insights help theology to lay aside idealized or linear visions of the past and thus enter into the truth of reality, which entails both greatness and limitation, holiness and fragility, continuity and rupture. It is precisely in this real, palpable history — often riddled with contradictions — that God chose to make himself known.

Ultimately, it is no coincidence that a deeper understanding of the mystery of the Church goes hand in hand with a return to its origins. This is prompted not by a mere desire for restoration, but by the search for authenticity. The Church awakens and renews itself by studying how it was born and what most deeply defines it. In this regard, Christian archaeology can provide a significant contribution by helping to distinguish what is essential from what is secondary, the original core from the later additions of history.

However, it is important to bear in mind that this is not about reducing ecclesial life to a cult of the past. True Christian archaeology is not a matter of sterile conservation, but of living memory. It is the ability to make the past speak to the present, and the wisdom of being able to recognize the role of the Holy Spirit in guiding history. In this sense, Christian archaeology can offer a common language, a shared foundation and a reconciled memory. It can help us recognize the multiplicity of ecclesial experiences, the variety of forms and the unity that exists within diversity. It is also capable of becoming a place of listening, a space for dialogue and an instrument of discernment.

_The value of academic communion_

In 1925, [Pius XI](https://www.vatican.va/content/pius-xi/en.html) established the Pontifical Institute of Christian Archaeology notwithstanding the economic difficulties and the reigning uncertainty of the post-war period. He acted with courage and foresight, confident in both science and faith. Today, a century later, his resolution is a cause for reflection. Do we too believe in the power of study, formation and memory? Are we willing to invest in culture despite today’s crises, to promote knowledge despite indifference and to defend beauty even when it seems irrelevant? Fidelity to the spirit of the founders means renewing efforts, rather than becoming complacent about what has already been achieved. It means training people who are capable of thinking, questioning, discerning and narrating. It means sharing, communicating and involving others, rather than confining oneself to elitist knowledge.

On this centenary, I would also like to reaffirm the importance of communion among the various institutions dedicated to archaeology. [The Pontifical Roman Academy of Archaeology](https://www.cultura.va/content/cultura/en/collegamenti/accademie-pontificie/archeologia.html), [the Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/pontifical_commissions/archeo/index.htm), [the Pontifical Academy _Cultorum Martyrum_](https://www.vatican.va/content/romancuria/en/pontificie-accademie/pontificia-academia-cultorum-martyrum/profilo.html) and the Pontifical Institute of Christian Archaeology each have their own specific role, but they all share the same mission. It is essential that they cooperate and communicate with each other, as well as provide mutual support. They should develop synergies, organize joint projects and promote international networks.

Christian archaeology is not a privilege for a select few, but a resource for everyone. It can offer unique contributions to humanity’s intellectual patrimony, inspire respect for diversity and promote culture.

Archaeology can also provide opportunities for fruitful cooperation with the Christian East. Shared catacombs and churches, as well as similar liturgical practices and converging martyrologies all constitute a spiritual and cultural heritage that are to be valued together.

_Education in memory, fostering hope_

In today’s fast-paced world, there is a tendency to forget and to consume images and words without reflecting on their meaning. The Church, on the other hand, is called to educate people in memory, and Christian archaeology is one of its most noble tools for doing so — not in order to take refuge in the past, but consciously to live in the present and work towards an enduring future.

Those who know their own history know who they are. They know where to go. They know whose children they are and the hope to which they are called. Christians are not orphans: we have a genealogy of faith, a living tradition and a communion of witnesses. Christian archaeology reveals this lineage and preserves its signs, interpreting them, recounting them and passing them on. In this sense, it is also a ministry of hope, for it shows that faith has already survived difficult times and resisted persecution, crises and changes. Faith has been renewed and regenerated, taking root in new peoples and flourishing in new forms. Those who study the origins of Christianity discover that the Gospel has always had a generative force, that the Church is always reborn, and that hope has never faded.

_\*\*\*_

I would like to invite the bishops, as well as leaders and guides in the areas of culture and education, to encourage young people, lay people and priests to study archaeology. It offers many formative and professional opportunities within ecclesiastical and civil institutions, in academic and social realms, as well as in the fields of culture and heritage conservation.

Finally, I address you, brothers and sisters, scholars, teachers, students, researchers, cultural heritage professionals and ecclesiastical and lay leaders. Your work is of immense value. Do not be discouraged by difficulties. Christian archaeology is a service, a vocation and a form of love for the Church and for humanity. Please continue your excavations. Continue to study, teach and recount history. Be tireless in your search, rigorous in your analysis and passionate in communicating with others. Above all, remain faithful to the true and profound purpose of your commitment: the endeavor to make visible the Word of life, bearing witness that God became flesh, that salvation has left its mark, and that this Mystery has become a historical narrative.

May the Lord bless you all, and may the communion of the Church sustain you. May the light of the Holy Spirit, who is living memory and inexhaustible creativity, inspire you, and may the Blessed Virgin Mary, who united the past and the future in one vision of faith by meditating on everything in her heart, protect you always.

_From the Vatican, 11 December 2025_

LEO PP. XIV

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

[\[1\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftnref1) Francis, [_Letter on the Renewal of the Study of Church History_](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/letters/2024/documents/20241121-lettera-storia-chiesa.html) _,_ 21 November 2024: _AAS_ 116 (2024), 1590.

[\[2\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftnref2) _Regulations for the Pontifical Institute of Christian Archaeology_ (11 December 1925), art. 1: _Rivista di Archeologia Cristiana_ of the Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology, 3 (1926), 21.

[\[3\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftnref3) Pius XI, Encyclical Letter _Lux Veritatis_ (25 December 1931), Preface: _AAS_ 23 (1931), 493.

[\[4\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftnref4) Cf. P. Saint-Roch, _Discours inaugural_: edited by N. Cambi and E. Marin, _Acta XIII Congressus Internationalis Archaeologiae Christianae,_ I, Vatican City 1998, 66-67.

[\[5\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftnref5) Francis, [_Letter to Cardinal Gianfranco Ravasi on the Occasion of the XXV Public Session of the Pontifical Academies_](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/letters/2022/documents/20220201-cardinale-ravasi.html) (1 February 2022): _AAS_ 114 (2022), 211.

[\[6\]](http://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/apost_letters/documents/20251211-nel-centenario-piac.html#_ftnref6) For example, the Creed contains a reference to Pontius Pilate, a historical figure that allows us to date the events remembered.
